Building Custom Controllers

A custom Controller is a user-authored coordination authority that plugs into the Conductor. Custom Controllers follow the same contract and lifecycle as built-in Controllers, allowing engineers to implement domain-specific policy, rate limiting, gating, or error-handling logic without modifying internals. Because custom Controllers are subject to the same voting protocol, ordering, and lifecycle rules as built-in Controllers, they extend pipeline capabilities without compromising its deterministic execution guarantees.

Every Controller—built-in or custom—implements ControllerContract<T> and is decorated with @VaultController. The Conductor discovers, validates, and invokes custom Controllers exactly as it does add-on Controllers.

Controllers do not transform state. They receive messages about pipeline attempts, successes, and failures, and respond with a vote that tells the Conductor how to proceed.

What You Need

A complete custom Controller consists of the following pieces:

  1. A Controller class decorated with @VaultController and implementing ControllerContract<T>.
  2. An options interface that defines the configuration the Controller accepts.
  3. A fluent API installer (installFluentApi) so engineers can configure the Controller with a chained method call on the FeatureCell.
  4. An optional extension interface with TypeScript module augmentation for the fluent API type.
  5. Registration in the FeatureCell declaration's Controller array.
The Voting Model

Controllers respond to pipeline messages by returning a vote. The Conductor collects votes from all registered Controllers and uses them to determine pipeline progression.

ControllerVote
Vote Description
Abstain The Controller has no opinion. The pipeline proceeds as if this Controller were not present.
Deny The Controller blocks the current attempt. The Conductor may revote the attempt later (for example, after a timer expires).
Abort The Controller permanently blocks the attempt. This acts as a circuit breaker and the attempt is not retried.
ControllerMessageType
Message Type Description
Attempt A new pipeline attempt is requesting permission to proceed.
Success An attempt completed successfully.
Failure An attempt encountered an error.
Step 1 — Define an Options Interface

The options interface describes the configuration your Controller expects. It is passed to the constructor via controllerCtx.controllerConfig. 

{{`export interface MyControllerOptions {
  /** Maximum number of concurrent pipeline attempts allowed. */
  maxConcurrent: number;
}`}}
Step 2 — Create the Controller Class

Decorate the class with @VaultController and implement ControllerContract<T>. The decorator metadata tells the Conductor the Controller's type, unique key, and whether it requires configuration. 

{{`import {
  ControllerClassContext,
  ControllerContract,
  ControllerMessageShape,
  ControllerMessageTypes,
  ControllerType,
  ControllerTypes,
  ControllerVote,
  ControllerVotes,
  defineControllerKey,
  FeatureCellBaseShape,
  VaultController
} from '@sdux-vault/shared';
import { Observable, of } from 'rxjs';

import { MyControllerOptions } from './my-controller.options';

@VaultController({
  type: ControllerTypes.Policy,
  key: defineControllerKey('Policy', 'MyController'),
  critical: false,
  wantsConfig: true,
  configKey: 'withMyController'
})
export class withMyController<T> implements ControllerContract<T> {

  // ── Static metadata (mirrored by the decorator) ──────────
  static readonly type: ControllerType;
  static readonly key: string;
  static readonly critical: boolean;
  static readonly wantsConfig: boolean;
  static readonly configKey: string;

  // ── Instance fields ──────────────────────────────────────
  readonly type = withMyController.type;
  readonly key: string;
  readonly critical = withMyController.critical;

  readonly #maxConcurrent: number;
  #activeCount = 0;

  // ── Fluent API installer ─────────────────────────────────
  static installFluentApi<T>(
    cell: FeatureCellBaseShape<T>,
    controllerConfigs: Map<string, unknown>
  ) {
    cell.withMyController = function (
      options: MyControllerOptions
    ) {
      controllerConfigs.set(
        withMyController.configKey, options
      );
      return this;
    };
  }

  // ── Constructor ──────────────────────────────────────────
  constructor(
    key: string,
    readonly controllerCtx: ControllerClassContext
  ) {
    this.key = key;

    const options =
      controllerCtx.controllerConfig as MyControllerOptions;

    if (
      typeof options?.maxConcurrent !== 'number' ||
      options.maxConcurrent < 1
    ) {
      throw new Error(
        '[vault] withMyController requires ' +
        'maxConcurrent (number >= 1).'
      );
    }

    this.#maxConcurrent = options.maxConcurrent;
  }

  // ── Message handler ──────────────────────────────────────
  handleMessage(
    msg: ControllerMessageShape<T>
  ): Observable<ControllerVote | void> {

    switch (msg.type) {
      case ControllerMessageTypes.Attempt:
        if (this.#activeCount >= this.#maxConcurrent) {
          return of(ControllerVotes.Deny);
        }
        this.#activeCount++;
        return of(ControllerVotes.Abstain);

      case ControllerMessageTypes.Success:
      case ControllerMessageTypes.Failure:
        this.#activeCount = Math.max(0, this.#activeCount - 1);
        return of(ControllerVotes.Abstain);

      default:
        return of(ControllerVotes.Abstain);
    }
  }

  // ── Lifecycle ────────────────────────────────────────────
  reset(): void {
    this.#activeCount = 0;
  }

  destroy(): void {
    this.#activeCount = 0;
  }
}`}}
Note

The static fields (type, key, critical, wantsConfig, configKey) are populated at runtime by the @VaultController decorator. Declare them as static readonly for type safety.

Decorator Metadata Reference

The @VaultController decorator accepts the following metadata:

ControllerMetaShape
Property Description
type: ControllerType

required

 The Controller category. Determines how the Conductor classifies and invokes the Controller. Use a value from ControllerTypes.
key: string

required

 Unique identifier for this Controller. Created with defineControllerKey('Domain', 'Name'). The key follows the format SDUX::Controller::Domain::Name. Used for diagnostics, DevTools visualization, and Conductor classification.
critical?: boolean

optional

 Indicates whether this Controller is critical. When true, any error in this Controller halts the pipeline.
wantsConfig?: boolean

optional

 When true, the Conductor passes the fluent configuration to the constructor via controllerCtx.controllerConfig. Defaults to false when not provided.
configKey?: string

optional

 The key used to look up the Controller's configuration from the fluent API config map.
needsLicense?: boolean

optional

 Indicates whether this Controller requires a valid license to execute. When true, the Conductor validates the license before invoking the Controller. Defaults to false when not provided.
licenseId?: string

optional

 The license identifier required for this Controller. Used by the Conductor to validate that the appropriate license is present.
Step 3 — Module Augmentation (Optional)

Add a module augmentation so the fluent API (cell.withMyController()) is visible to TypeScript. 

{{`import { MyControllerOptions } from '../options/my-controller.options';

declare module '@sdux-vault/shared' {
  interface FeatureCellFluentApi<T> {
    withMyController?(options: MyControllerOptions): this;
  }
}`}}
Step 4 — Register the Controller

Pass the Controller class to the FeatureCell declaration's Controller array. Then use the fluent API to provide configuration. 

{{`// app.config.ts
provideFeatureCell(
  MyCellService,
  {
    key: 'my-cell',
    initialState: {}
  },
  [],
  [
    withMyController   // register in the controller array
  ]
);

// my-cell.service.ts
this.vault
  .withMyController({ maxConcurrent: 3 })
  .initialize();`}}
 
{{`import { FeatureCell } from '@sdux-vault/core';
import { withMyController } from './with-my-controller.controller';

export const myCell = FeatureCell(
  MyCellToken,
  {
    key: 'my-cell',
    initialState: {}
  },
  [],
  [
    withMyController   // register in the controller array
  ]
);

myCell
  .withMyController({ maxConcurrent: 3 })
  .initialize();`}}
Controller Lifecycle

The Conductor manages each Controller through a predictable lifecycle:

  1. Construction — The Conductor instantiates the Controller, passing the assigned key and a context object containing the configuration (if wantsConfig is true).
  2. handleMessage — Called each time the pipeline needs a vote. The Controller inspects the message type and trace ID, then returns an Observable<ControllerVote>.
  3. reset — Called when the pipeline resets. Clear internal counters, maps, or timers.
  4. destroy — Called when the FeatureCell is destroyed. Release all resources.
Extending an Existing Controller

You can extend a built-in Controller class to inherit its base logic and override specific methods. Apply a new @VaultController decorator with a unique key and configKey so the Conductor treats your subclass as a distinct Controller. 

{{`import {
  ControllerTypes,
  defineControllerKey,
  VaultController
} from '@sdux-vault/shared';
import { withDelayController } from '@sdux-vault/addons';

@VaultController({
  type: ControllerTypes.Policy,
  key: defineControllerKey('Policy', 'CustomDelay'),
  critical: false,
  wantsConfig: true,
  configKey: 'withCustomDelay'
})
export class withCustomDelayController<T>
  extends withDelayController<T> {

  // Override handleMessage to add logging,
  // adjust delay logic, or add conditional bypasses.
}`}}
Note

The new @VaultController decorator replaces the parent's metadata entirely. The Conductor will register your subclass under the new key and config key.

Extensible Controller Types

The following Controller types are available for custom Extensions. Each type corresponds to a coordination category that the Conductor recognizes.

Extensible Controller Types
Controller Type Description
Error Controllers that define error-handling policies for the pipeline. Only one Error Controller may be active per FeatureCell.
Policy Controllers that enforce pipeline execution policies such as rate limiting, circuit breakers, concurrency gates, or approval workflows.
ReplayGlobalError Controllers that coordinate the replay of previously captured global errors back into the pipeline.
Stepwise Controllers that coordinate stepwise bus interactions, mediating multi-phase pipeline resolution through the voting model.
Restricted Controller Types

Not all Controller types are available for custom Extensions. The Conductor enforces a strict boundary between core pipeline infrastructure and the extensible Controller surface. Controllers that belong to core pipeline internals are managed exclusively by the Conductor and are silently removed if provided in the FeatureCell Controller array.

The following Controller types are restricted and cannot be registered as custom Extensions:

Restricted Controller Types
Controller Type Reason
CoreAbstain Manages the core abstain voting protocol. Reserved for internal use by the Conductor.
License Enforces license validation for pipeline execution. Reserved for internal use by the Conductor.

If a custom Controller is registered with any of the restricted types listed above, the Conductor removes it during pipeline initialization. No error is raised; the Controller is silently excluded from pipeline execution.

Licensing

Custom Controller extensions are available exclusively with a purchased Pro plan. The Conductor validates the active license during pipeline initialization and silently excludes custom Controllers when a valid Pro license is not present. For licensing details and plan options, see the product page.
